title: Your Video Is Getting Swiped Away Before the Point Arrives
markdown:
# Your Video Is Getting Swiped Away Before the Point Arrives

You post a short video, watch the first few seconds back, and feel a small win: the edit is clean, the lighting is fine, the topic is useful. Then the retention graph falls off a cliff before you have said the useful part.

That drop is not always a content problem. Often it is a first-three-seconds problem.

People do not swipe because they have weighed your argument and rejected it. They swipe because they cannot yet tell why they should stay. A hook has one job: make the right person recognize the subject and feel a reason to wait for the next sentence.

## The opening is a promise, not an introduction

Compare these two starts for a video about better freelance pricing:

> "Today I want to talk about a mistake I see a lot of freelancers make when they price their work."

> "If clients keep saying yes too fast, your price may be too low."

The first sentence asks for patience before it gives the viewer anything. The second names a situation a freelancer may already recognize. It also leaves a question open: how can a quick yes be bad news?

That is the shape you want. Be specific about who the video is for, name the friction they feel, then create a believable gap between what they assume and what you will show.

## Find the sentence your viewer is already thinking

Before you write a hook, finish this sentence without trying to sound clever:

"The person I want to reach keeps thinking: ________."

For a fitness coach, it might be: "I train all week and still feel like I am starting over every Monday."

For a product designer, it might be: "Everyone says the onboarding is simple, so why do new users still disappear?"

For a creator who teaches video editing: "My cuts are faster now, but the videos still feel slow."

The blank gives you material with some life in it. A viewer does not wake up wanting a video called "Three tips for engagement." They wake up annoyed by a thing that happened to them. Start there.

## Use the first line to remove doubt

A stranger should understand the subject on one listen. If your opener needs context, it is late.

Weak: "This changed how I think about content."

Clearer: "Your tutorial loses viewers when the answer arrives after the intro."

The clearer line does not have more polish. It has a subject, a consequence, and a target. It tells a tutorial creator that this is about a familiar failure, not a vague personal revelation.

Try reading your hook with the sound off. If the first on-screen sentence could belong to almost any creator in almost any niche, it is not carrying enough weight. Add the actual object: the cold email, the meal plan, the client call, the camera settings, the checkout page. Specific nouns do more work than excited adjectives.

## Put a real contrast in the first three seconds

Clarity gets attention. Contrast gives it somewhere to go.

The easiest contrast starts with a belief your viewer already holds, then turns it slightly:

- "More edits will not fix a slow opening."
- "Your before-and-after video is starting at the wrong moment."
- "The best part of your tutorial should not be the last thing you say."

Each line points at a common habit and promises a better explanation. None needs a wild claim. In fact, a hook that feels too theatrical creates a second problem: viewers wait for the trick, realize there is no trick, and leave anyway.

The contrast has to match the video that follows. If the hook says the intro is the problem, show the intro. If it says a popular tactic is hurting retention, explain the mechanism and offer a replacement. A hook earns a few more seconds. The rest of the video has to deserve them.

## Draft several hooks before you choose one

Most first hooks are summaries. That is normal. Do not publish the first summary just because it is true.

For one video, write five starts from different angles:

1. Name the viewer's mistake: "You are explaining the context before you earn attention."
2. Name the surprising consequence: "A useful video can fail before the useful part begins."
3. Turn a familiar belief: "Being clearer can make your hook shorter, not softer."
4. Use a sharp question: "Why do viewers leave right before your best tip?"
5. Start inside the moment: "At two seconds, the viewer has already decided whether your tip is worth hearing."

Then test each one against four questions:

- Does the viewer know the topic immediately?
- Would the right person feel addressed?
- Is there a tension that the video will resolve?
- Can you deliver on it without padding the next thirty seconds?

The winner is rarely the most dramatic line. It is the one that makes the next line feel necessary.

## Build the visual and spoken hook together

Short-form video gives you two entrances at once: what people see and what they hear. Do not make them compete.

If you say, "Your before-and-after video is starting at the wrong moment," open on the weak before shot, not a smiling introduction. If you say, "Clients who say yes too fast may be underpaying you," put the quote on screen. The image should make the spoken line easier to grasp, not repeat it as decorative text.

You do not need a frantic cut every half second. You need the first frame to answer, "What am I looking at?" and the first sentence to answer, "Why should I care?" A messy desk, a stalled analytics graph, an unopened cart, or a side-by-side edit can do more than a generic pointing-to-text clip.

## Make the hook a small editing habit

Before posting, take ten seconds for a ruthless check. Delete greetings. Delete "in this video." Delete the sentence that explains why you decided to make the video. Move the useful sentence to the front, then see whether it still sounds like something a person would say out loud.

If you are stuck, use Hook Lab to generate and pressure-test directions against the swipe problem you are trying to solve: https://capafy.ai/agent/8123079349?ct=hooklab_blog

The goal is not to trick anyone into staying. It is to stop making the right viewer work so hard to recognize that the video is for them. Give them the problem they know, a claim worth checking, and a fast path into the proof. The swipe becomes less automatic when the opening finally has something to hold onto.
